title: How One Used Uniform Fooled an Entire Empire
description:
In October 1906, a 57-year-old shoemaker with a criminal record put on a captain's uniform he had bought piece by piece from junk dealers. Within a few hours, real soldiers were following his orders, the mayor of Köpenick was under arrest, and the town's cash was in two mail sacks. He signed the receipt with the name of his old prison director.

This is the true story of Wilhelm Voigt, the Captain of Köpenick: how he pulled it off, how he was caught, why the whole world laughed, and the passport he said he was really after.

Facts used: Wilhelm Voigt was born in Tilsit, East Prussia, in 1849 and was first sentenced at 14; he spent about 29 years of his life behind bars, the last stretch for trying to break into a court's cash box, and was released in February 1906. Ordered out of Wismar and banned from Berlin, he stayed in Berlin anyway and bought the pieces of a 1st Foot Guards captain's uniform from second-hand dealers in Berlin and Potsdam. On October 16, 1906, he took command of four guardsmen returning from the military swimming baths at Plötzensee and six more from a shooting range, gave them beer and one mark each, and took them by train to Köpenick. At the town hall, at about 2:46 PM, he posted guards on the exits, had the post office stop calls to Berlin for an hour, and arrested Mayor Georg Langerhans. Treasurer von Wiltberg counted out a little over 4,000 marks; Voigt left with about 3,500 in two mail sacks and signed the receipt "von Malzahn", the name of the director of his last prison. A 2,000-mark police reward was offered, and Köpenick added 1,000. He was arrested at breakfast on October 26 with about 770 marks spent, and on December 1, 1906 a Berlin court gave him four years. Kaiser Wilhelm II pardoned him in August 1908, after about 20 months. He became a celebrity (a gramophone record, a waxworks figure, stage tours), wrote a memoir in 1909 saying he had only wanted a passport, although the Köpenick town hall had no passport office. He settled in Luxembourg, received a Luxembourg passport in May 1910, and died there in 1922.

The spoken orders are dramatized from the reported ones. The scenes are an animated dramatization.
